notes: In this episode, Leandro talks with Chris Mayer, author of 100 baggers and portfolio manager at the Woodlock House Family Capital Fund. Chris talks about his investment philosophy and both also discuss Copart (CPRT)
transcript:
Hey, anchors, today I will be talking with Chris Mayer, co-founder and portfolio manager of Woodlaug House Family Capital Fund.
Most of you might know him for his book 100 Baggers, which outlines the characteristics of stocks of companies that have managed to compound 100x over long periods.
It's a great book and definitely one I would put on my list of required books to read by an investor.
Chris's background is undoubtedly impressive, but what I like the most about him is that I think that his investment style is fairly significant.
similar to that of best anchor stocks. And the fact that he's always open to discussion.
Welcome, Chris, and thanks for taking the time. Yeah, thank you. Thank you for having me on.
Leandro, it's good talk to you. Okay, so I think the best thing we can start off is,
why don't you give, like, a background of yourself? Because I think most people here know you
for the book, 100 baggers. Right. But you, and well, also your recent writings had would love
Woodlockhouse blog, but I think you started your career writing a different blog, and that led eventually
to becoming a professional investor. So can you tell us a bit more about this?
Yeah, I mean, my, my background is kind of an unconventional path to money management. So, yeah, I was in
in corporate banking for 10 years from 94 to 2004, 2004. And during that time, I was always
writing on the side. And finally, in 2004, I started my own newsletter. And then that newsletter
I had, you know, I had a model portfolio and I have stocks that I tracked kind of very similar to what you're
doing. And that did very well over 10, 10 year period of time. And so eventually I joined the, um, started working
with the Bonner family office in 2016. So the Bonner's were a newsletter publisher.
And when I was writing my newsletter, I had made a deal for them.
to publish it shortly after I started. It was only about six months or so. So that, that worked out
out really well. I left the banking job and just was able to write my letter and traveled all over the
the world and wrote four of my books and including 100 baggers. And so that was very good.
And then 2016 started work with the family office. And then that led to me eventually
proposing to them start a fund, which they seeded. And we started in 2019. So that's, that's
the short answer. Well, that that's very interesting. I think you can be considered like a player of the
gig economy, but like, before it was mainstream, like now, because everyone is jumping on it.
That's right. I mean, I remember when I first started my newsletter, I mean, I had physical copies. I actually
mailed to people. It's sort of funny to think about it. It really wasn't, really wasn't
that, you know, that was kind of the way newsletters were at that time. And there definitely weren't,
there was not the substacks and all the blogs and everything that we have now. So it's definitely
proliferated. And it's probably easier now to get started in that, in that business. And a lot
easier to get eyeballs, you know, through Twitter and, and then the rest of it.
Yeah, definitely. It's just impressive that by saying sending physical copies,
you were able to make a living out of it. That's quite interesting. Yeah, quite interesting.
Okay, so now jumping to to investment-related topics directly, I think I have to start by asking you a question
that might open up the rest of the conversation. How would you define your investment style?
Yeah, I mean, I think it's very close to what I wrote about in 100 baggers.
That's basically the approach I take, which is to focus on the underlying compounding of the
companies themselves, the businesses themselves, return on capital, their ability to reinvest and
continue to do that over a long period of time. So I definitely focus on insider ownership with something else
I talked about in the book. A lot of the companies I own are founder-led or at least their significant
significant skin in the game and good balance sheets and really taking that long view looking to hold on
businesses for a decade and allowing that kind of compounding to work.
So there's a lot of pieces and parts to go into that, but that's how I would basically characterize it.
And has this style been static or have you modified it throughout the years? For example,
when when you started your newsletter, was the style the same or have you make like some
modification because I feel that as investors we are constantly evolving. So, for
example, Warren Buffett shifted from cigar butts to some sort of quality investing. So curious to know
if your investment style has changed much or it has remained fairly stable. No, I'd say it's changed a lot.
Yeah, I've made that same migration. So when I started, I was much more the kind of traditional
value investor with a heavy focus on multiples and buying things below book value and
that kind of stuff. And gradual over time, you know, started to migrate more toward the quality side. And
so I think that's a pretty traditional arc. I think a lot of people kind of go through that same
path over time. And it really is just driven by my experience and learning more about
businesses and studying more about businesses. I mean, you start to really appreciate the power of just owning
owning a really good business and sitting on the shares for a long time and what that can do versus
if you're so valuation focused, then you are forced to do a lot of trading. You're forced to come
up with a lot of ideas.
and you're going to make mistakes.
And it's just seems a harder path to go.
Now, there's people, of course, have been very successful with it, so I'm not denigrating that path in particular.
But just my, my pattern, my migration has been much more toward that quality side.
And so it's become a lot cleaner and simpler.
I remember early on, I used to do just about everything.
I remember doing special situations and being involved with turnarounds and all kinds of things.
And now, over all this time,
my filter is really tightened up. It's a really much simpler focused approach.
And did you, while you were doing those special situations or focusing more on, on valuation, did you have
any painful experience that made you shift to more quality investing?
Yeah, I think, well, I know that one particular
defining moment, I would say, was during the 2008 crisis when there were lots
and lots and lots of cheap stocks around everywhere.
I mean, you could buy, I remember buying stock that was profitable and it was market cap was below the net
cash. But these were not very good businesses. And what wind up happening is, you know,
I would buy these cheap stocks and they may do very well, but then two years or so later,
you wind up selling them. And then when you look back, you see that really, if you had bought
some of the best businesses at that time, you would have done so much better. And you would
still, you would still own those names. Like, thinking about you could have bought, you know, Microsoft,
I mean, even MasterCard Visa, the two that stand out to me in 2008. I don't know what they're
up since, but it's a crazy number. And so I started looking back.
I'm thinking, wow, you know, next time there's a crisis, I'm not going to just go to the cheapest
things. I'm just going to buy the best businesses that I, that I know, and the ones that I've always admired
and wanted to own, but perhaps never quite got cheap enough. And then that migration started to happen
then. And it was just kept going. This more and more and more, I would focus on quality. And then
my understanding of quality has also evolved over time. I mean, it's become more refined
it changed itself. So that was kind of the, that was what did it. And so, you know, and I got to put that in
practice again in 2020, March of 2020, things were going nuts. And what I did then was I didn't just
go and automatically buy the statistically cheapest stocks. I went and picked up two businesses
that I've long admired, one being copart, which I think we'll talk about later, and the
other being HICO. And the nice thing about that is I still own both. And so, and I think I will own them both
for a very long time. So that, that's kind of how that shift happened. And also, I'll also just throw one more
thing in there, Leandro. Sorry. You know, writing the book, a hundred bag of book itself also had a great
impact on me. So I did all that research in 2014. And the book came out of
2015. And 2014, I remember I met with Chuck Akre in Middleburg, Virginia, and
uh, talked to him. And this is when the pieces really started to come together. So it took a while
for the really, really sink in so that, you know, that the, I would really focus on this,
the exclusion of other things and resist the siren call of, of the statistically cheap stocks.
But that is really those, those were the two episodes, I think, that we really,
really pushed me on the way.
Yeah, I think what's complex here is that if people that look at statistically cheap stocks can
find data to support their view, and people who focus on quality can find data to focus, like, to support
their view. So I think that at the end, what's important is to do your own research and find your own
own data, because if not, I think you could be misled into thinking that one thing,
works better than the other. And actually, what you might do, like, what you must do is find
something that works for you. And you, you mentioned, you mentioned, you mentioned there that.
Yeah, I mean, just to add to that, I mean, that's, I think when you pointed out there is really,
really important, really important, which is that you have to have an investment style that
matches your temperament, because if you try to do something that you really
don't believe in or that doesn't fit your temperament, it's not going to work
for you. The market's going to test you. And as soon as what you're doing stops working,
you'll, you know, abandon it an exact wrong time. So that's a really important point. And I just
enforce that. Yeah. And you talked about that how you have refined your filter for high quality companies.
I feel that it's something that it's quite subjective. Well, like everything in investing,
but quality, some people see, I look at a company and would say,
it's very high-quality companies and other people would think that it's not not a high-quality company.
So if you had to choose three characteristics of a high-quality company, what would they be and why?
Well, I think what's high-quality business? It starts with high returns on capital in some way.
And, you know, you have to use whatever metrics are appropriate for that particular business,
but the general numbers are, you know, return on capital employed, return on invested capital,
something like that.
And that's number one.
High quality business will have high returns and it makes intuitive sense when you think about it.
And second trade is the ability to continue to earn those returns over a long period of time.
So it's not just that a business can have two or three really good years and then it suffers
and then it goes and has a couple more good years.
but somebody who's a business that can consistently earn those returns over a long period of time.
And that's those two things alone are really the key to the whole 100-bagger algorithm, if you want to call it that.
And when I look at all those companies that return to 100-fold or more over a long period of time,
they all had this ability.
And so those are two most important things, I would say.
Yeah.
Yeah.
And I, I think, what?
what you're saying basically is like a company that has a moat or a competitive advantage that
allows it to compound capital at higher rates than competition.
Yeah, because that's kind of the components, right?
Once I say those two things, well, those are just kind of like outcomes.
And then the more important thing is how do you identify them really?
Because you can look at, anybody can just look at the numbers, but that's not going to necessarily
do it.
Because like you mentioned, to be able to do that, you have to have a very strong competitive
moat. You have to be able to fend off competition because obviously those high returns are going
going to attract competitors. People are going to try to replicate what you're doing. And if you can't
defend that business against that, then that's not particularly good investment. So that's one. I mean,
the other point, you know, one thing that when I talk about my investment process has been refined
refined is I put much, much more weight on qualitative factors than I did before. And that is really
understanding management and the alignment, how well they're aligned with stockholders. Because
you're going to own a business over a decade, they're going to allocate a lot of capital. And business generates
cash, they're going to have to invest it, figure out what to do with it. And those decisions are crucial
to long-term returns. And you can have a business, a management team really fritter away
returned by making poor decisions. So that is very key. More and more I've come to
understand investing is really about people.
And based on the competitive advantages, I had one question for you that I'm quite interested in seeing
your, what you reply. I think in now we live in an era that it's dominated by technology. And there are a lot
of companies that people think that have strong competitive advantages, but these competitive
advantages are based on technology. So my feeling is that it takes something more than just
technology to really build a durable competitive advantage.
Because I think that there are many companies that, thanks to technology, are able to scale really fast
and basically it into your mode.
So I would like to know what's your feeling around technological modes, so to say. And if you look
look for something else on technology, or you are actually comfortable holding a company whose mode is
mostly technological.
Yeah, I mean, I'm inclined to agree with you.
and it may reflect a bias of my own, but I prefer some other moat other than just purely a technology,
or I also don't particularly like modes that are just purely built around a brand.
I mean, I want to have some more tangible evidence or support for high return.
So I love, you know, like network effects are very difficult to break or something that's
built around a physical mode.
And, you know, like Copart, which we probably thought we're going to talk about, and Old Dominion freight
lines is another one where they have a, where their advantage over competition is partly in an actual
physical network that they have built over a long period of time, and that is very, very difficult,
if not impossible for a competitor to replicate at this point.
So those kind of competitive advantages are really ones that I,
that I love to look for.
And those are ones that are, you know, very difficult to break versus if you're just relying on a technology,
it seems to me, there's always a risk somebody comes along with something better, and then you're stuck.
Yeah. And based on one, you just commented on network effects.
Yesterday, I had a conversation on Twitter that I think that according to Morningstar,
network effects are the strongest competitive advantage. But I, I, I, I,
differ a bit in that I think a network effect is really, really strong when one of the sites
has the burden in power with respect to the other side because I think we'll talk about it later,
but co-party is another example of that, but or Visa or MasterCard where obviously they have, like, they can do
do what they want because it's not the merchant who has the burgan in power.
And I think, I think I came to this conclusion based on, well, you can see what
happened with TikTok or what's happening with other, for example, dating apps that are eating
into matches territory.
And I feel that when the both parts have like a similar bargaining power, then it's not as strong
because someone could, could come, another platform could come, and as long as they are able to
convince one of the parts, then the other has like very, very little switching costs.
Mm-hmm.
Mm-hmm.
Mm-hmm.
Yeah, I mean, I think what you're saying too there basically is that not all network effects are the same.
And I would agree that that's true almost with all these moats, even with a moat based in some kind of physical advantage that, you know, even those modes, some moats are better than others.
So it's really hard to generalize about moats.
And sometimes, you know, I'm always intrigued by situations whether it doesn't appear to be any moat.
And yet the company consistently earns returned on capital that way exceed the industry.
And so, you know, that, that could be evidence of some sort of hidden moat or some other
mode that's not necessarily obvious.
And sometimes that can be a cultural advantage that's very difficult to replicate.
I mentioned Old Dominium freight lines.
That's the one that comes to mind because you look at it.
It's LTL trucking.
It's not necessarily seemed like it's anything special.
But they also have, there's some interesting cultural things there that make them different.
You know, they have the lowest turnover of any.
trucking firm in the industry by quite a lot and there there's other aspects there
that that add to that so more like brown and brown is another one I own as an insurance broker is not
any particular obvious moat when you look at the insurance brokers and compare them against each
other but you know brown and brown has the industry leading free cash flow conversion rate and
they've done very very well over a long period time so there's you know it's kind of like a signal that
there may be something there that they're doing different.
They're their competitors that there is some kind of moat there that isn't necessarily obvious.
So there's lots of different modes and lots of different ways to talk about them.
And sometimes it's hard to generalize.
It really have to dig into the specific company in its ecosystem and figure out, you know,
why this business is able to do what it's done for so long.
I think we can we can agree that identifying a mode is,
requires quite a bit of judgment on the investor side. And it's somewhat well, it's like
all the qualitative factors of a company, it's somewhat subjective.
Yeah. I think you may be identifying the mode today is not as subjective, but understanding how it will
evolve in the future, which is what's really important. It's quite subjective because every investor would
look at the industry dynamics differently or what the company, the moves the company is making
today. I think that's one of the reasons why, like, most investors build diversified
portfolios. I mean, we, we always have to acknowledge that we could be wrong in identifying modes.
So how do you, how do you go about diversification versus concentration? Do you tend to diversify or
are you a fairly concentrated investor? I am fairly concentrated. I am fairly concentrated. So right now I have
10 stocks. And running a concentrated portfolio like that impacts what kinds of
businesses you invest in to begin with. So there's a whole bunch of things that are just off limits.
So, you know, companies that have a lot of leverage or any company where there's a decent
risk of a permanent impairment or capital loss of some kind has got to be off the table.
And different portfolios can run and may run differently. If you had 30 stocks, you might be able
to take, you know, more of a flyer and have a package of, say, I don't know, uranium stocks or something,
but something that you would never make a 10, 10 stock portfolio. It's kind of your portfolio,
uh, structure portfolio also has to match not only your SMAT match your psychology,
but also has to match up with your approach.
So, yeah, I'm pretty concentrated.
10 stocks and I try to keep them in different businesses so that if I own, you know, I won't,
I won't typically double up on anything.
If I own Brown and Brown, I'm not going to own another broker or if I own, you know, I own
co-part, I'm not going to own the competitor as well.
I usually won't make one choice and try to keep them so that there are not, you know,
I'm not unintentionally doubling up on things somehow and manage the exposure that way.
Also, you know, there's wide geography.
I have things on stocks all over the world.
And so that's how I handle that.
I think that's things that's evolved over time, you know, over time.
In the beginning, I would have been terrified having a position of, say, 10%.
But over, you know, I've been in this now for almost 30 years.
You get more comfortable with what you own and how to get
that comfort and you gain more confidence in what you can do.
And so, yeah, I think naturally, you kind of gravitate towards picking fewer names, but raising that bar
on what you own.
Yeah, I think something that you just said is often overlooked by investors that if you have a fairly
concentrated portfolio, if you just look at the weights of the companies, that doesn't mean that the
portfolio is not diversified because actually you can be, you can have 25% positions and be much more
concentrated that someone that has 10 positions with 10% each because the businesses are different and are
uncorrelated with each other. I think it goes down also to the to the company level. So if you own a company
that only has one revenue stream, well, obviously, obviously, that's not a diversified company.
but I can have a significant stake in a company that has many business lines.
I think you, we talked a bit about, we have talked a bit about atlas Copco, the Swedish industrial
toolmaker.
Like, if you look at their business, well, obviously, you would say, no, it's just industrial as well,
but they cater like to a lot of industries and a lot of different use cases.
So you are buying, you're actually buying a diversified company, even.
if you put a significant stake of your portfolio in it, it would be, I would consider it to be quite
diversified.
Yeah, I would agree with that.
I mean, you know, like if you own Berkshire Hathaway, it's quite a bit different than owning a company
that only has one business and does one thing.
Or like, you know, we own Constellation software as another name we have in common,
and that's, you know, where they have 500 plus businesses or something.
So, yeah, you can definitely kind of get the benefits of diversification even within
in one business if they have multiple, multiple lines of business for sure.
Now, now I want to jump to another topic that it's very relevant to our days, which is macro.
I want to know if you focus on the broader economy when making investment decisions or you just
focus on the resilience of a company during a tough period.
Yeah, I mean, I definitely focus on the resilience of the businesses.
So that's, you know, important part of my filters, having very strong balance.
sheet. So, you know, of the 10 companies I own, I think seven of them have no net debt
and maybe a few others say very low levels of debt. So that's important. And the fact that I've done
all this work on their business, the competitive position, and so they should prove to be durable
companies and have proven to be durable companies in the past. And so I'm not one to sit around and
try to predict what the economy is going to do and or what interest rates are going to do
or whatever. I mean, part, part of the challenge here is if you're going to be a long-term investor,
you really want those big multi-baggers that we dream about, the hundred baggers, it requires you
to sit still. It requires you to own a good business for a long period of time. And that means you're going
to have to own it through recessions, through periods where the economy is weak, and
you're going to have to own it through the periods where the stocks draw down, you know, third or more.
And so that that is the path I've chosen to take.
And you talked about that you filter companies based, for example, on financial strength.
How do you source your investment ideas? Because I feel that there are like thousands, tens of
thousands of publicly traded securities. And a good portion actually might seem high
quality at first site. So is there something that you look at first and then from then on you do more research
or you actually do research from the starting point? Because I typically used screeners. But I feel
that a screener gives you an image of like a point in time. I see it as a balance sheet, so
to say, like you can put growth metrics. Yeah. But it may be you're missing a lot of companies
that are high quality and maybe are going through a tough period and they won't appear on the screen.
Right. So how do you go about filtering investments? Yeah. Well, I mean, I would say it's not necessarily
systematic. I, you know, I've been in business for a long time. So I know there's a bunch of companies I
like and I kind of keep an eye on. I would say one of the big filters for me that's easy as
I always start with the proxy, any kind of company that I'm going to look at. And I have
use screens in the past, too, to get some new names, new ideas. But the first stop for me is always
the proxy. And that will tell you what the, who the largest shareholders are. I'll tell you the
insider ownership. So that's a thing that's important for me in my fund. I talk about
all the time, having skin in the game. And so that's something I'm definitely looking for.
So if it's a company doesn't, you know, the management team owns one percent of
shares, it's probably not, I'm not going to spend any time on it. So that's the first filter
that knocks out a lot of stuff. And the second one that knocks out a lot of things is being very,
very strict on the balance sheet. So if they, you know, anything with leverage on it, I'm not going to
spend much time on it either. And I understand now, you know, people will say, but they always
want to say, but what about X, Y, and Z companies that have been very successful.
And even though management has never owned a lot of shares or even though they run
with a leverage balance sheet. And, you know, that's fine. I know that I'm going to miss a lot of things.
But like you say, the investment universe is thousands and thousands of securities and you have to figure
out a way to kind of filter it and manage it down to something you can handle. And I have, you know,
reasons for picking the kinds of things I've picked. There's lots of research that shows how insider
ownership leads to outperformance. And intuitively, you understand that strong balance sheets
will get you through the tough cycles. And if I'm not going to be trading around recessions and hard
periods, I want to make sure that my businesses can get through that without having to raise money by issuing
more shares at an inopportune time or something like that. So those are two of my biggest filters.
And that knocks out a lot of stuff right away. Yeah, I guess that if you hold 10 companies,
you have to be very, very strict on your filters, because if not, you will end up diluting
the quality of the, of the portfolio.
Yeah.
Okay, so I think we have now covered most of the topics related to the company.
So now it's time to jump to valuation.
So how do you approach valuation?
Do you use discounted cash flow models, maybe an inverse discounted cash flow models?
Do you use multiples?
Yeah, my value, we?
I try to keep it very simple. So what I typically will do is I look at what the return on capital is what the
return on capital is, what the reinvestment rate is, and then cast out free cash flow or earnings over
the next five and 10 years, and then put some multiple on that, and then discount back to
whatever the IRA is and I want to have at least 15% IRAR out to five years. I want
want to basically double my money out to five. That's kind of how I think about it. And when I think
about the returns and reinvestment, I'm trying to get something I think is probable. You know,
it looks like I have high degree of confidence that they will be able to hit those numbers over the
next five years. And, and then you, you know, you try to build in some cushion there so that you, if
